# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v9)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; present day (spring transitioning to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford harbor towns, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere); Secondary locations: San Francisco, New York, Eastern Prussia, Germany, Hamburgh; French locations (D——, Manosque, Sisteron, Hautes-Alpes, Paris, Italy, Durance, Château-Arnoux, Senez, Briançon, Aix, Draguignan, Embrun, Chastelar, Arche, Barcelonette, Jauziers, Tuiles, Joug-de-l'Aigle, Ubaye, Ubayette, Ollioules, Nice, Piédmont, Couloubroux, Pompierry)
- Atmospheric details: Rain threatening; wind with salt and tar smell; frosted hedges; smoke lying flat; bees in lavender; dog barking; bell for vespers; children chasing hoop shrieking; gulls over fish heads; chalk sun on forge wall; road rutted and puddled after thaw; light going early; baker's boy late at oven; cart with turnips; carts creaking past wells

## Main Characters and Relationships

**M. Charles Myriel / Monseigneur Bienvenu (Bishop)**
- French aristocrat; family ruined by Revolution; emigrated to Italy at very beginning of Revolution; wife died in Italy
- Became priest, then Bishop of D——; encountered Napoleon in Paris circa coronation epoch
- Redistributes entire 15,000 franc yearly State salary across 23 charitable categories; retains 1,500 francs yearly for personal sustenance
- Within less than a year, became treasurer of all benevolence; considerable sums passed through his hands
- Philosophy: society culpable for poverty and ignorance; dark soul results from darkness created by society, not individual malice
- **Attended condemned murderer's execution; spent entire day in prison; mounted tumbril and scaffold with prisoner, becoming father, brother, friend. Upon knife falling, told sufferer: "God raises from dead whom man slays; rejected one finds Father once more. Pray, believe, enter into life: the Father is there." Sufferer became radiant.**
- **Upon return, entered deep moral crisis: phantom of social justice tormented him; subject to lugubrious monologues questioning his role in witnessing state-sanctioned death; ruminated on scaffold as monstrous instrument, accomplice of executioner.**
- **Daily life: Sleeps little; morning meditation one hour; says mass; breaks fast on rye bread dipped in milk; receives secretary and vicars-general; devotes remaining time to sick and afflicted; works in garden and writes, calling both "gardening"**
- **Midday stroll in country or town when weather fine; often enters lowly dwellings; walks alone, buried in thought, supporting himself on long cane**
- **Presence warming and luminous; children and old people come to doorsteps for him as for the sun**
- **At half-past eight evening sups with sister: extraordinarily frugal repast of vegetables boiled in water and oil soup. When curés visit, Madame Magloire serves excellent fish or fine game.**
- **After supper converses half hour with Mademoiselle Baptistine and Madame Magloire; retires to write on loose sheets and margins. Man of letters; left behind five or six curious manuscripts including dissertation comparing three texts on Genesis.**
- **Called to bedside of sick and dying at any hour; understands this his greatest duty. Knows how to sit silent for long hours beside grieving widows and bereaved mothers.**
- **Household: ground floor three-room structure (dining-room, bedroom, oratory with no exit except through bedroom); alcove with bed in oratory for visiting country curates; hospital pharmacy converted to kitchen and cellar; stable in garden holds two cows; invariably sends half their milk daily to hospital sick**
- **Furniture sparse and austere: six silver knives, forks, and soup-ladle retained from former possessions; two large candlesticks of massive silver inherited from great-aunt; holds wax candles, placed on chimney-piece; lighted and set on table when Bishop dines with guests. Iron hospital bed with green serge canopy; bookcase cupboard with glass doors. Two oval-framed portraits on wall: Abbé of Chaliot and Abbé Tourteau (appointed by king April 27, 1785).**
- **Red brick chambers washed weekly; exquisite cleanliness—sole luxury Bishop permits.**
- **Garden: four alleys in cross-form radiating from tank with circumferential walk skirting white enclosing wall. Three plots used by Madame Magloire for vegetables; fourth planted by Bishop with flowers and few fruit-trees. Bishop plants and tends flower-beds; loves flowers rather than studying them. When Madame Magloire remarked flower plot useless, Bishop replied: "The beautiful is as useful as the useful. More so, perhaps."**
- **House has no locked doors day or night; any passer-by can push open at any hour. Bishop's philosophy written on Bible margin: "This is the shade of difference: the door of the physician should never be shut, the door of the priest should always be open."**
- **When worthy curé asked whether leaving door unfastened risked misfortune, Bishop touched his shoulder gently and said: "Nisi Dominus custodierit domum, in vanum vigilant qui custodiunt eam," Unless the Lord guard the house, in vain do they watch who guard it.**
- **Bandit incident: After destruction of Gaspard Bès's band in Ollioules gorges, lieutenant Cravatte took refuge in mountains then reappeared near Barcelonette. Seen at Jauziers, Tuiles; hid in Joug-de-l'Aigle caverns; descended through ravines of Ubaye and Ubayette; pushed far as Embrun, entered cathedral, despoiled sacristy.**
- **In midst of terror, Bishop arrived making circuit to Chastelar. Mayor urged him to retrace steps; Bishop replied: "What would they say to bishop who was afraid?" He traveled mountain on mule-back alone without sister or Madame Magloire; encountered no one; arrived safe with shepherds; remained fortnight preaching, administering sacrament, teaching, exhorting.**
- **Upon return from shepherds' circuit, found large chest deposited in presbytery by two unknown horsemen containing cope of cloth of gold, mitre ornamented with diamonds, archbishop's cross, magnificent crosier—all pontifical vestments stolen month previously from Notre Dame d'Embrun treasury. Paper in chest read: "From Cravatte to Monseigneur Bienvenu."**
- **Told Baptistine and Magloire: "Well! was I in right? Poor priest went with empty hands, returns with hands full. Set out bearing only faith in God; brought back treasure of cathedral." That evening before bed said again: "Let us never fear robbers nor murderers; those petty dangers from without. Let us fear ourselves. Prejudices real robbers; vices real murderers. Great dangers lie within ourselves."**
- **To his sister on precautions against fellow-man: "Sister, never a precaution on the part of the priest, against his fellow-man. That which his fellow does, God permits. Let us confine ourselves to prayer, when we think that a danger is approaching us. Let us pray, not for ourselves, but that our brother may not fall into sin on our account."**
- **Regarding stolen cathedral treasure: An obscure note found among Bishop's papers, couched in terms: "The question is, to decide whether this should be turned over to the cathedral or to the hospital."** It consisted of very handsome things, very tempting things, and things well adapted to be stolen for benefit of unfortunate.
- **Bishop travels to visit old member of the Convention dwelling three-quarters hour from city, far from any hamlet or road, in hidden turn of wild valley. Path had disappeared under growth of grass; locality spoken of as dwelling of hangman.**
- **Upon arrival near lair: Bishop strode over ditch, leaped hedge, made way through fence of dead boughs, entered neglected paddock, took few steps with boldness, and suddenly at extremity of waste land and behind lofty brambles, caught sight of the cavern.**
- Makes thirty-two curacy, forty-one vicarship, and two hundred eighty-five auxiliary chapel visits; traveled on ass to Senez when purse dry
- Conversation gay and affable; puts himself on level with companions; laughs like schoolboy; relatively short stature
- Provençal; speaks all dialects of south; perfectly at home in thatched cottage and mountains
- Not to be rebuffed when charity questioned; caught wealthy givers with gentle raillery; told avaricious Marquis de Champtercier to "give [poor people] to me"

**Mademoiselle Baptistine** (Bishop's sister)
- Long, pale, thin, gentle creature; embodiment of respectability
- Never was pretty; whole life succession of holy deeds; acquired beauty of goodness
- Yearly income 500 francs for personal wants; subsists on shared 1,500 francs with bishop and servant
- **Overheard and preserved Bishop's self-reproaching monologues about scaffold and death; witnessed his deep moral crisis**
- Occupies first floor with Madame Magloire; renounced dream of elegant furniture
- **In letter to Madame the Vicomtess de Boischevron reveals: Initially feared his dangers ("he is terrible"); now accustomed to his risks. Makes sign to Madame Magloire not to oppose him. Carries off Magloire, enters chamber, prays for him and falls asleep; at ease knowing if anything happened, she would go to good God with her brother and bishop. Has cost Magloire more trouble to accustom herself to his "imprudences," but habit now acquired. They pray together, tremble together, fall asleep. If devil entered house, would be allowed to do so; always some one stronger than they are with them; good God dwells here.**

**Madame Magloire** (Bishop's servant)
- Only servant in household; grumbled about financial arrangement; likes to call Bishop "Your Grace"
- Subsists on shared 1,500 francs yearly; takes advantage of visiting curés to serve excellent fish and game
- **Had frights from unlocked door but eventually accustomed herself to Bishop's openness to wanderers; now shares confidence or acts as though she shares it**
- Attends household cleaning; discovered paintings beneath washed-over paper; contemplates silver knives, forks, soup-ladle with delight daily
- Occupies first floor with Baptistine

**Mrs. Hurtle** (now Mrs. Fisker, departed)
- American woman, formerly engaged to Mr. Montague; forgave him but remained deeply wounded
- Final meeting: threw herself into Montague's arms, declared love "with my very heart of hearts," covered his face with kisses; he responded with cold constraint
- Collapsed prone on floor afterward; became unusually gracious to Mrs. Pipkin
- Departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York; became Mrs. Fisker very soon after arrival at San Francisco
- Never to revisit England; carries miniature portrait of Mr. Montague

**Mr. Montague (Paul)**
- English gentleman; weak regarding women; abandoned Mrs. Hurtle for English girl
- Will marry Marie Melmotte and remain in England
- Soon after Hetta's arrival in Suffolk, came to Carbury
- Received warmly by Roger; Roger keeps promise to treat him as brother
- Roger told him much of land, tenants, labourers, farm income, necessity of living within means

**Marie Melmotte** (now Mrs. Fisker, departed)
- Young, beautiful daughter of deceased Melmotte; concerned about propriety regarding Mrs. Hurtle
- Became engaged to Hamilton K. Fisker; understood at Hampstead
- Departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York; became Mrs. Fisker very soon after arrival at San Francisco
- Determined never to revisit England; reminiscences not happy

**Mr. Hamilton K. Fisker** (departed)
- American associate; passionate but grew less wise as bigger; fixed departure September 3rd
- Married Marie Melmotte very soon after arrival at San Francisco

**Madame Melmotte** (departed)
- Widow of Melmotte; mother of Marie; recently widowed, engaged to marry Herr Croll
- Departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York; determined never to revisit England

**Herr Croll** (departed)
- Associate of American establishment; Germanic accent; astute character analyst
- Married Madame Melmotte; departed Liverpool September 3rd for New York

**Lady Carbury (now Mrs. Broune)**
- Mother of Sir Felix and Hetta; financially burdened
- Agreed Mr. Broune's proposition: Sir Felix receives £175 per year if travels to Germany; nothing if remains
- Initially rejected Mr. Broune's marriage proposal two or three months ago, chiefly because of son's position
- After Sir Felix's exile confirmed, Mr. Broune renewed proposal; she accepted by kneeling at his feet with face buried on his knees
- Before winter was over, became wife of Mr. Broune; took his name; experienced thorough reaction of spirit; world changed from perfect blank to rose-colored
- Viewed Mr. Broune as one of considerable ones of world; believed being his wife was career enough
- Knows her son well; gave him five-pound note at parting; Mr. Broune expressed angry energy upon learning this
- Mrs. Broune's Tuesday evenings much more regarded by literary world than Lady Carbury's

**Sir Felix Carbury**
- Son of Lady Carbury; brother of Hetta; exhausted funds; no tradesman will give credit
- Assented to Mr. Broune's proposition; duly introduced to Rev. Septimus Blake
- Spent last sovereign on farewell dinner at Beargarden
- Before end of August, embarked from Hull for Hamburgh with Blake family
- Mother gave him five-pound note at parting

**Mr. Broune**
- Great editor; powerful and influential man; very obstinate, reasonable, somewhat hard of heart
- Proposed marriage to Lady Carbury two or three months ago; she declined
- Changed manner toward her; less gentle than before
- Persuaded her to allow Sir Felix to travel to Germany; threatened homelessness and financial deprivation if he remained
- Offered £175 per year if Sir Felix went
- Between him and Mr. Blake, ensured Sir Felix's departure from Hull before end of August
- Renewed marriage proposal after son's exile; said circumstances changed
- Expressed angry energy upon learning Lady Carbury gave Sir Felix five-pound note
- Believed he never loved her better than when she refused him, because he thought she did so from propriety
- Became "quite another person"—different from earlier gentle behavior

**Hetta Carbury**
- Daughter of Lady Carbury; sister of Sir Felix; does not want her mother's company
- Engaged to marry Roger Carbury; wedding fixed for following spring
- Invited by Mrs. Yeld (Bishop's wife) to stay at palace in Suffolk
- Left London before hearing of mother's engagement with Mr. Broune
- Will spend autumn and possibly winter in Suffolk to become accustomed to Roger in his new capacity
- After arrival at palace, Roger visited and walked with her in garden for couple of hours two days after Bishop's conversation

**Roger Carbury**
- Landowner in Suffolk; gentleman with considerable property (Carbury estate)
- Loves Hetta Carbury; she agreed to marry him; wedding set for following spring
- Believed Paul Montague unfit to marry Hetta due to his conduct with Mrs. Hurtle
- Will not tell tales against Montague
- Resigned to never marrying or having children of his own
- Conceived idea that Hetta should spend autumn and winter in Suffolk to become accustomed to him
- Induced Mrs. Yeld to invite her down to palace; told much of his story to Bishop
- Bishop discouraged him from settling property on Hetta, warning he might yet marry and citing King Lear
- Abandoned idea of settling property on Montague's children but remained resolute in determination to make himself subordinate to cousin's interests
- Conquered his regrets; looks forward to Hetta's and Paul's presence at Carbury as source of all future happiness
- Makes Paul welcome as though he were his brother, Hetta as though she were his daughter
- Resolved that all anger is gone; threw hands up as though scattering indignation to air
- Holds property as steward for those to come after him
- Told Hetta she will teach herself to regard him as her best and closest friend
- Assured her Marie will come and enjoy it; that is settled
- Promised after Marie's visit, Carbury will be Hetta's home so she learns to care about and love the place
- Acknowledged Carbury will be Hetta's home really in future; she will be Squire of Carbury when he is gone
- Could not bring himself to say Paul Montague should be Squire of Carbury
- Hopes "all our troubles are over now," referring to himself and Hetta

## Secondary Households and Marriages
- Stenson household (Torton): Matho and Ismira Stenson; 4 children: Kassa, Orrald, Pelde, Gazek
- Stenworth household (Torton): Havus and Fewyn Stenworth; 4 children including Yera, Lurald, Davus, Pelde
- Corrley household (Kelmere): Gadan and Zalis Corrley; 3 children: Rinelle, Kadan, Taric
- Thornmere household (Ostcombe): Islan and Vesmira Thornmere; 2 sons: Jotho, Isric
- Stenenridge household (Dunstead): Rozek and Luena Stenenridge; 2 children: Thizek, Pewyn
- Corrford household (Dunstead): Yedan and Nylia Corrford; 3 children: Ulrald, Marald, Yewyn
- **Ulrald Corrford and Kassa Stenson are married; live in Dunstead**
- **Marald Corrford and Fenelle Lindmere are married; live in Dunstead**
- **Gazek Stenson and Pelde Stenworth are married; live in Torton**
- **Taric Corrley and Kassa Stenson are married; live in Kelmere** [NOTE: contradiction with above; clarification needed]
- **Luwyn Brackick and Lurald Stenworth are married; live in Kelford** [NOTE: Lurald appears in both Stenworth household and married couple]

## Other Characters
- The Bishop and Mrs. Yeld: Roger's friends; prudent wisdom; invited Hetta
- Rev. Septimus Blake: Clergyman; traveled with Sir Felix
- M. le Cardinal Fesch: Powerful church figure; Napoleon's uncle
- Napoleon: Emperor; encountered Bishop Myriel
- M. Géborand: Wealthy retired merchant, usurer; amassed two millions; never gave alms until hearing sermon on charity; afterward gave sou to six beggar-women every Sunday
- Marquis de Champtercier: Wealthy, avaricious; simultaneously ultra-royalist and ultra-Voltairian
- Cravatte: Bandit lieutenant; succeeded Gaspard Bès; stole pontifical vestments from Notre Dame d'Embrun; returned them to Bishop via unknown horsemen with note
- **Old member of the Convention (G——): Dwelling three-quarters hour from city in hidden wild valley. Mentioned with horror in little world of D——; nearly voted for death of king (quasi-regicide). Member of Convention when people called each other "thou" and said "citizen." Almost a monster; had been terrible man. People wondered why not brought before provost's court on return of legitimate princes. Besides being nearly regicide, was also atheist, like all the rest of those people. Gossip of town treats him as "gossip of geese about vulture." Bishop experiences that sentiment which borders on hate, expressed by word estrangement, yet finds idea of this estrangement strange, impossible, and almost repulsive after moment's reflection.**

## Key Events
- Sir Felix exiled to Germany/Eastern Prussia before end of August
- Lady Carbury married Mr. Broune before winter was over
- Hetta invited to stay at palace in Suffolk; left before hearing of mother's engagement
- Roger visited Hetta at palace; they walked in garden
- Paul came to Carbury; Roger received him warmly
- September 3rd: Madame Melmotte, Marie, Mrs. Hurtle, Fisker, Herr Croll departed Liverpool for New York
- Marie and Fisker married very soon after arrival at San Francisco
- **Bishop attended condemned murderer's execution and entered deep moral crisis regarding state-sanctioned death**
- **Bishop traveled alone to mountain shepherds despite bandit danger; witnessed return of stolen ecclesiastical vestments from Cravatte via mysterious horsemen**
- **Bishop now visits old member of the Convention dwelling in hidden wild valley cavern**

## Themes
- Religious devotion and charitable duty; practical compassion superseding institutional role
- **The moral weight of state-sanctioned execution; justice versus mercy; conscience and torment of witnessing institutional violence**
- **Universal human dignity and divine law transcending human law**
- Redemption through charity and unexpected grace
- **The beautiful as legitimate human need, not mere luxury; contemplation and aesthetic appreciation as spiritual practice**
- **Trust in Divine providence over human security measures; openness to strangers and wanderers**
- **Moral estrangement and prejudice; overcoming initial revulsion through personal encounter**
- Resignation and acceptance of life's disappointments
- Property, inheritance, and future generations
- Male honor and keeping promises despite personal pain
- Simplicity and austerity as spiritual practice
